enable.e: From Middle English enablen, equivalent to en- + able.
enable.g: To make somebody able (to do, or to be, something); to give sufficient ability or power to do or to be; to give strength or ability to.

enact.e: From Middle English enacten, from en-, from Old French en- (“to cause to be”), from Latin in- (“in”) and Old French acte (“perform, do”), from Latin actum, past participle of ago (“set in motion”).

encampment.e: From encamp (“to establish a camp or temporary shelter”) + -ment (suffix forming nouns denoting actions or their results).
encampment.g: A place where people (such as displaced people, soldiers, or travellers) encamp, that is, stay in tents or other temporary structures; a cam

enchanter.e: From Middle English enchantour, from Old French enchanteor (Modern French enchanteur), from Latin incantātor (“enchanter; spellcaster; conjurer”), from incantāre (“to sing, to consecrate with spells”). Equivalent to enchant + -er.

enchantment.e: From Middle English enchauntement, from Old French enchantement.
enchantment.g: The act of enchanting or the feeling of being enchanted.

enclose.e: From Middle English enclosen, inclosen, from Middle English enclos, from Old French enclose, feminine plural past participle of enclore, from Vulgar Latin *inclaudō, *inclaudere, from Latin inclūdō (doublet of include), from in- (“in”) + claudō (“to shut”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂u- (“key, hook, nail”). Equivalent to en- + close.
enclose.g: To surround with a wall, fence, etc.

encompass.e: From Middle English encompassen. By surface analysis, en- + compass.
encompass.g: To form a circle around; to encircle.

encounter.e: From Middle English encountren, from Anglo-Norman encountrer, Old French encontrer (“to confront”), from encontre (“against, counter to”), from Late Latin incontrā (“in front of”) itself from Latin in (“in”) + contrā (“against”).
encounter.g: To meet (someone) or find (something), especially unexpectedly.

encourage.e: From Middle English encouragen, encoragen, from Anglo-Norman encoragier, from Old French encoragier. By surface analysis, en- + courage.
encourage.g: To mentally support; to motivate, give courage, hope or spirit.

encroach.e: From Middle English encrochen, from Old French encrochier (“to seize”), from Old French en- + croc (“hook”), of Germanic origin.

encrust.e: From French incruster, from Latin incrustare, from in- (“in”) + crustare (“to cover with a crust”). By surface analysis, en- + crust.
encrust.g: To cover with a hard crust.

encumber.e: From Middle English encombren, from Old French encombrer, from en- + combrer (“to hinder”) (See cumber). By surface analysis, en- + cumber.
encumber.g: To load down something with a burden.

encumbrance.e: From Middle English encombraunce, from Old French encombrance, from encombrer.
encumbrance.g: Something that encumbers; a burden that must be carried.

end.e: From Middle English ende, from Old English ende, from Proto-West Germanic *andī, from Proto-Germanic *andijaz (“end”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂entíos (“forehead; front”), from *h₂ent- (“face; forehead; front”), from *h₂en- (“on, onto”).
end.g: The terminal point of something in space or time.

endamage.e: From Middle English endamagen, from Old French endamagier.

endanger.g: To put (someone or something) in danger; to risk causing harm to.

endeavor.e: Endeveren is from (putten) in dever (“(to put oneself) in duty”), from in + dever (“duty”), partially translating Middle French (se mettre) en devoir (de faire) (“(to make it) one's duty (to do), to endeavour (to do)”) (from Old French devoir, deveir (“duty”)).
endeavor.g: A sincere attempt; a determined or assiduous effort towards a specific goal; assiduous or persistent activity.

ending.e: From Middle English ending, endyng, endende, from Old English endiende, from Proto-Germanic *andijōndz, present participle of Proto-Germanic *andijōną (“to end”), equivalent to end + -ing.

endless.e: From Middle English endeles, from Old English endelēas (“endless”), from Proto-Germanic *andijalausaz (“endless”), equivalent to end + -less.

endlessly.e: From Middle English endelesly, from Old English endelēaslīċe; equivalent to endless + -ly.
endlessly.g: In an endless manner; continuously without limit.

endorse.e: Alteration influenced by Medieval Latin indorsare of Middle English endosse, from Old French endosser (“to put on the back”), from Latin dossum, alternative form of dorsum (“back”), from which also dorsal (“of the back”).
endorse.g: To express support or approval, especially officially or publicly.

endow.e: From Late Middle English endowen, endouen, enduen, indouen, indw (“to provide with assets, a livelihood, or privileges; to bestow, grant; (figuratively) to favour; to endow”), from Anglo-Norman endouer, from Old French en- (prefix meaning ‘in, into’) + douer (“to endow”) (from Latin dōtāre (present active infinitive of dōtō (“to endow”)).
endow.g: To give property to (someone) as a gift; specifically, to provide (a person or institution) with support in the form of a permanent fund of

endue.e: From both of the following: Chiefly sense 1: Late Middle English induen (“to clothe (someone); to assume or take on (an appearance)”), from Latin induere, the present active infinitive of induō (“to put on (clothes, etc.); to assume (a part)”), from indu- (an archaic variant of in- (prefix meaning ‘in.
endue.g: Senses relating to covering or putting on.

endurance.e: From Middle French endurance, from Old French endurance. Morphologically endure + -ance.
endurance.g: The measure of a person's stamina or persistence.

endure.e: From Middle English enduren, from Old French endurer, from Latin indūrō (“to make hard”).
endure.g: To continue or carry on, despite obstacles or hardships; to persist.

enemy.e: From Middle English enemy, enemye, enmy, borrowed from Old French enemi, anemi (Modern French ennemi), from Latin inimīcus, from in- (“not”) + amīcus (“friend”).
enemy.g: Someone who is hostile to, feels hatred towards, opposes the interests of, or intends injury to someone else.

energy.e: From Middle French énergie, from Late Latin energia, from Ancient Greek ἐνέργεια (enérgeia, “activity”), from ἐνεργός (energós, “active”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”). The sense in physics was coined by English polymath Thomas Young in 1802 in his lectures on Natural Philosophy.
energy.g: The impetus behind all motion and all activity.

enfold.e: Alteration of earlier infold, from Middle English infolden, equivalent to en- + fold.
enfold.g: To envelop and wrap up something.

enforce.e: From Middle English enforcen, from Old French enforcier, from Late Latin infortiāre, from in- + fortis (“strong”).
enforce.g: To keep up, impose or bring into effect something, not necessarily by force.

engage.e: From Middle English engagen, from Old French engagier (“to pledge, engage”), from Old French en- (“in, under”) + gage (“pledge”), from Frankish *wadi (“pledge”), from Proto-Germanic *wadją (“pledge, guarantee”), from Proto-Indo-European *wedʰ- (“to pledge, redeem a pledge; guarantee, bail”), equivalent to en- + gage.

engine.e: From Middle English engyn, from Anglo-Norman engine, Old French engin (“skill, cleverness, war machine”), from Latin ingenium (“innate or natural quality, nature, genius, a genius, an invention, (in Late Latin) a war-engine, battering-ram”), related to ingignō (“to instil by birth, implant, produce in”).
engine.g: A large construction used in warfare, such as a battering ram, catapult etc.

engraft.e: From earlier ingraft, equivalent to en- (“in”) + graft.
engraft.g: To insert, as a scion of one tree or plant into another, for the purpose of propagation; graft onto a plant

engrave.e: From earlier ingrave, equivalent to en- + grave (“to carve, engrave”).
engrave.g: To carve text or symbols into (something), usually for the purposes of identification or art.

engraving.g: The practice of incising a design onto a hard surface, by cutting grooves into it.

enhance.e: From Middle English enhauncen, anhaunsen, from Anglo-Norman anhauncer (“enhance, raise”), from Vulgar Latin *inaltiāre (“raise”), derived from Latin in + altus (“high”). The /h/ in Old French was taken from haut (“high”), where it resulted from Frankish influence.

enjoin.e: From Middle English enjoinen, from Old French enjoindre (“to join with”), from Latin iniungo (“to attach”), a compound of in- (“into” “upon”) and iungo.
enjoin.g: To lay upon, as an order or command; to give an injunction to; to direct with authority; to order; to charge.

enjoy.e: From Middle English enjoyen, from Old French enjoier, anjoier, enjoer (“to give joy, receive with joy, rejoice”), equivalent to en- + joy.
enjoy.g: To receive pleasure or satisfaction from something.

enlarge.e: From Middle English enlargen, from Old French enlargier, enlargir. By surface analysis, en- + large.

enlighten.e: Formerly also inlighten, from Middle English enlightenen, inlightnen, a hybrid formed from inlighten (“to enlighten, illuminate”), from Old English inlīhtan, onlīhtan, enlīhtan (“to enlighten, illuminate, give light to, give sight to”) and lightnen (“to enlighten, illuminate”) (equivalent to light + -en).

enmity.e: From Middle English enemyte, from Old French enemisté, ennemistié, from Late Latin, Vulgar Latin *inimīcitās, *inimīcitātem, from Latin inimīcus (“enemy”). By surface analysis, en(e)m(y) + -ity.
enmity.g: The quality of being an enemy; a hostile or unfriendly disposition.

enormous.e: From Latin ēnormis. An assimilated form of ex- (“out of”) + norma (“rule, norm”) + -ous.
enormous.g: Deviating from the norm; unusual, extraordinary.

enough.e: From Middle English ynogh, from Old English ġenōg (“enough”), from Proto-Germanic *ganōgaz (“enough”) (compare Scots eneuch, West Frisian genôch, Dutch genoeg, German genug, Low German (ge)noog, Danish nok, Swedish nog, Icelandic nógur).
enough.g: Sufficient; all that is required, needed, or appropriate.

enquire.e: From Old French enquerre, from en- + querre (“to search, to look for”), from Latin quaerere, of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Italic *kʷaizeō, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeh₂- (“to acquire”).

enquiry.e: From Middle English enquery, from the Old French verb enquerre, from Latin inquīrō, composed of in- (“in, at, on; into”) + quaerō (“to seek, look for”), of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Italic *kʷaizeō, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeh₂- (“to acquire”).

enrage.e: From Old French enrager, enragier, from rage. Equivalent to en- + rage.

enraged.e: From Middle English. By surface analysis, enrage + -ed.
enraged.g: Angered, made furious, made full of rage.

enrich.e: From Middle English enrichen, from Anglo-Norman enrichir and Old French enrichier. By surface analysis, en- + rich.

enroll.e: From Middle English enrollen, from Anglo-Norman enroller; by surface analysis, en- + roll.
enroll.g: To enter (a name, etc.) in a register, roll or list

ensample.e: From Middle English ensaumple (noun) and ensaumplen (verb), from Old French ensample.
ensample.g: An example; a pattern or model for imitation.

ensign.e: From Middle English ensigne, from Old French enseigne, from Latin īnsignia, nominative plural of īnsigne, meaning marked, distinguished.
ensign.g: A badge of office, rank, or power.

ensue.e: From Old French ensu-, stem of some conjugated forms of ensuivre (“follow close upon, come afterward”) (French ensuivre), from Latin īnsequere, from īnsequi (“to pursue, follow, follow after; come next”), from in- (“upon”) (see in-) + sequi (“follow”) (see sequel).

ensure.e: From Middle English ensuren, from Anglo-Norman enseurer, from Old French seur (“sure”).
ensure.g: To make sure or certain of something (usually some future event or condition).

entangle.e: From Middle English entanglen (“to involve in difficulty”, “to embarrass”). Equivalent to en- + tangle.
entangle.g: To tangle up; to twist or interweave in such a manner as not to be easily separated.

enter.e: From Middle English entren, from Old French entrer, from Latin intrō (“enter”, verb), from intrā (“inside”). Has been spelled as "enter" for several centuries even in the United Kingdom, although British English and the English of many Commonwealth Countries (e.g.
enter.g: To go or come into an enclosed or partially enclosed space.

enterprise.e: From Old French via Middle English and Middle French entreprise, feminine past participle of entreprendre (“to undertake”), from entre (“in between”) + prendre (“to take”), from Latin inter + prehendō, see prehensile.
enterprise.g: A company, business, organization, or other purposeful endeavor.

entertain.e: From Middle English entertenen, from Middle French entretenir, from Old French entretenir, from entre (“among”) + tenir (“to hold”), from Latin inter + teneō (“hold, keep”). For the noun, compare French entretien. Sense of answering a phone call in Malaysian English is influenced by Malay layan “to serve, to attend to or engage with something”.
entertain.g: To amuse (someone); to engage the attention of agreeably.

entertainment.e: From Middle English entretenement (“support, maintenance”), from Old French entretenement; see entertain. Morphologically entertain + -ment.
entertainment.g: An activity designed to give pleasure, enjoyment, diversion, amusement, or relaxation to an audience, no matter whether the audience partici

enthrone.e: From en- + throne; compare earlier enthronize, inthronize.
enthrone.g: To put on the throne in a formal installation ceremony called enthronement, equivalent to (and often combined with) coronation or other cere

entice.e: From Middle English enticen, from Old French enticier (“to stir up or excite”), from a Vulgar Latin *intitiāre (“I set on fire”), from in- + titiō (“firebrand (tool)”), from Proto-Italic *tītjō (“heating”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *teih₁- (“to become hot, melt or to end”).
entice.g: To lure; to attract by arousing desire or hope.

enticeth.g: third-person singular present simple form of entice

entire.e: From Middle English entere, enter, borrowed from Anglo-Norman entier, from Latin integrum, accusative of integer (“whole”).

entirely.e: From Middle English entyerly, entierly, enterely, entyreliche, equivalent to entire + -ly.
entirely.g: To the full or entire extent.

entirety.e: From Middle English enterete, from Old French entiereté, from Latin integritās, from integer (“complete, whole”).
entirety.g: The whole; the complete or amount.

entrails.e: From Middle English entraille, entrailles, from Old French entrailles, from Vulgar Latin intrālia, from Latin interānea, from interāneus, from inter.

entrance.e: From Middle French entrance (“entry”). Replaced native Middle English ingang (“entrance, admission”), from Old English ingang (“ingress, entry, entrance”).
entrance.g: The action of entering, or going in.
To delight and fill with wonder.

entrap.e: From Middle French entrapper, entraper, from Old French entraper, antraper (“catch in a trap”), equivalent to en- + trap.
entrap.g: To catch in a trap or snare.

entry.e: From Middle English entre, from Old French entree (feminine past participle of the verb entrer, Modern French entrée). From Latin intrō.

entryway.g: An opening or hallway allowing entry into a structure; a pathway allowing entry into a locality or region.

envelop.e: From Middle English envolupen, from Old French anveloper, envoluper (modern French envelopper), from en- + voloper, vloper (“to wrap, wrap up”) (compare Italian -viluppare; Old Italian alternative form goluppare (“to wrap”)) from Vulgar Latin *vuloppare (“to wrap”), from Proto-Germanic *wlappaną, *wrappaną (“to wrap, roll up, turn, wind”).

envie.g: To vie; to emulate; to strive.
A strong desire or craving, especially for (a particular kind of) food.

envious.e: From Middle English envious, from Anglo-Norman envious, from Old French envieus, envious (modern French envieux), from Latin invidiōsus; more at envy.
envious.g: Feeling or exhibiting envy; jealously desiring the excellence or good fortune of another; maliciously grudging.

environ.e: From Middle English enviroun (“round about in a circle or ring; all around”), from Anglo-Norman enviroun, environ, and Middle French enviroun, environ, from Old French environ (“around, surrounding; about, approximately, roughly”) (modern French environ), from en- (prefix meaning ‘in; into’) + viron (“circuit; circumference, compass.

From Middle English envirounen, enviroun (“to surround in a circle or ring, or on the perimeter; to beset, besiege; to cover, enclose, envelop; to provide a setting or surrounding to; to move in a circle; to move around the perimeter; to go, move, or wander about (a place); to fill or pervade (a place); to run all the way through”).
environ.g: To encircle or surround (someone or something).

envision.e: From en- + vision, from Latin visionem (“a thing or sight seen”).
envision.g: To conceive or see something within one's mind. To imagine.

envoy.e: From French envoyé (“envoy, messenger”), from envoyer (“send”).
envoy.g: A diplomatic agent of the second rank, next in status after an ambassador.

envy.e: From Middle English envie, from Old French envie, from Latin invidia (“envy”), from invidere (“to look at with malice”), from in- (“on, upon”) + videre (“to look, see”).
envy.g: Resentful desire of something possessed by another or others (but not limited to material possessions).
